Crucified
KROO-si-fide
v. (past part.)
From Latin crucifigere, to fasten to a cross, from crux (cross) and figere (to fix). Webster 1828: nailed to a cross; put to death on a cross; mortified or subdued, as the flesh. The Romans reserved the punishment for slaves and rebels; Cicero called it the most cruel and shameful of penalties.

Biblical Definition

Crucified names both the historical death of Christ and the believer’s union with that death, and the New Testament will not let the two be separated. Paul reduced his entire preaching programme to the first: For I determined not to know any thing among you, save Jesus Christ, and him crucified (1 Corinthians 2:2). Not Christ in general but Christ under the curse, hanging on a tree, bearing wrath — that is the message, and Paul deliberately chose it over the rhetorical wisdom Corinth prized. But the same apostle speaks of himself in the same tense: I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me (Galatians 2:20). The believer did not merely benefit from the cross; he was on it in his Substitute, and the life he now lives is a life lent to a dead man. Romans states the consequence for indwelling sin: our old man is crucified with him, that the body of sin might be destroyed, that henceforth we should not serve sin (Romans 6:6). Crucifixion was slow, and so is mortification, but the verdict is already passed. Finally the cross severs the believer from the world in both directions: the world is crucified unto me, and I unto the world (Galatians 6:14) — each is a corpse to the other, and Paul will glory in nothing else.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines CRUCIFIED as nailed to a cross; put to death on a cross; and, in the figurative scriptural sense, mortified, subdued, or destroyed as to the power of sin and the affections of the flesh.

expand to see more

CRUCIFIED, pp. — Nailed to a cross; put to death by nailing the hands and feet to a cross.

Subdued; mortified; destroyed as to its dominion; as, the flesh with its affections and lusts.

Made dead to; separated by the cross from; as, the world is crucified to the believer.

In the passive scriptural sense, having died with Christ so that the old man no longer reigns.

From Latin crux, a cross, and figo, to fix — the root also of cross, crucial, and excruciating.

Key Scripture

1 Corinthians 2:2 — "For I determined not to know any thing among you, save Jesus Christ, and him crucified."

Galatians 2:20 — "I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me: and the life which I now live in the flesh I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself for me."

Romans 6:6 — "Knowing this, that our old man is crucified with him, that the body of sin might be destroyed, that henceforth we should not serve sin."

Galatians 6:14 — "But God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by whom the world is crucified unto me, and I unto the world."

Modern Corruption

The moral-influence and moral-example theories of the atonement keep the crucifixion and delete its substance, and the modern complaint that penal substitution amounts to divine child abuse attacks the Trinity as much as the atonement.

expand to see more

Abelard’s moral-influence theory, revived in nineteenth-century liberalism and standard in progressive evangelical writing today, holds that the cross demonstrates God’s love and thereby moves men to repent, but effects no propitiation. The New Testament forecloses this. If Christ crucified merely displays love, then 1 Corinthians 2:2 is a strange thing to build a ministry on, Galatians 3:13 has no meaning when it says He was made a curse for us, and 1 John 2:2 is unintelligible when it calls Him the propitiation for our sins. A display of love that averts no wrath is not love toward men in danger; it is theatre. The cross demonstrates love precisely because it accomplishes substitution — Romans 5:8 makes the demonstration depend on the death being for sinners.

The charge that penal substitution is cosmic or divine child abuse assumes an unwilling victim and two separate wills. Both assumptions are false. The Son says I lay down my life, that I might take it again. No man taketh it from me, but I lay it down of myself (John 10:17-18), and the Father and the Son are one God of one undivided will, so the covenant of redemption is not a transaction between two parties but the eternal purpose of one God executed by the Persons in their proper offices. Where the objection succeeds is against a caricature in which an angry Father is placated by a reluctant third party; it has no purchase on Chalcedonian Christology, and the objection is generally advanced by writers who have already abandoned the classical doctrine of God.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek stauroo (G4717), to crucify, to impale on a stake; sustauroo (G4957), to crucify together with; stauros (G4716), a cross; Hebrew talah (H8518), to hang, as of one hanged on a tree under the curse.

expand to see more

Greek stauroo (G4717) — to fasten to a stake or cross; the ordinary verb for the Roman execution (1 Corinthians 2:2).

Greek sustauroo (G4957) — to crucify together with; used of the two thieves and of the believer’s union with Christ (Romans 6:6; Galatians 2:20).

Greek stauros (G4716) — a cross, an upright stake; by metonymy the whole doctrine of the atonement (Galatians 6:14).

Hebrew talah (H8518) — to hang; he that is hanged is accursed of God (Deuteronomy 21:23), the verse Paul cites in Galatians 3:13.

Greek anastauroo (G388) — to crucify afresh; the apostates of Hebrews 6:6 crucify to themselves the Son of God afresh.

Usage

"Jesus Christ, and him crucified (1 Corinthians 2:2) — the deliberate narrowing of apostolic preaching."

"I am crucified with Christ (Galatians 2:20) — the believer’s union with the death he did not die."

"The world is crucified unto me, and I unto the world (Galatians 6:14) — a double severance, both ways."
